title: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
summary: How an LLM server schedules every iteration with continuous batching, accounts for KV cache memory, avoids fragmentation with block tables, and decides when to admit, preempt, swap or recompute.
outcomes: Explain the roles of the scheduler, KV cache manager and model executor in one engine step, and where CPU overhead hides
Explain why iteration-level scheduling with selective batching beats request-level batching
Measure a server with TTFT, ITL and TPOT percentiles over a load sweep, and avoid common benchmarking mistakes
Compute KV bytes per token, KV pool size and how many sequences fit, including models with sliding-window layers
Compare contiguous and paged KV allocation in terms of reserved, internal and external waste
Choose between reservation, preemption, swapping and recomputation for a given workload
Choose a request ordering policy (FCFS, predicted-length SJF, VTC fairness, priority) for a workload
Build an engine simulator with a block manager, token budget and recompute preemption

lessons.title: Inside an inference server: one engine step at a time

blocks.md:
Your GPT can generate text with a `for` loop: run the model, sample a token, append it, repeat. A serving system faces a harder problem. Thousands of requests arrive at random times, each with a different prompt length and an output length nobody knows in advance, and all of them must share one GPU's memory.

Recall from the GPU course: **prefill** runs the whole prompt through the model in one compute-bound pass, **decode** then produces one token per pass and is limited by memory bandwidth, and batching many sequences shares each weight read. This course is about the software that decides, every few milliseconds, which sequences form that batch and where their memory lives.

Both papers this course leans on split the server the same way. Orca (Yu et al., OSDI 2022) has a **request pool**, a **scheduler** and an **execution engine**. vLLM (Kwon et al., SOSP 2023), the paper behind the open-source vLLM engine, has a **centralized scheduler**, a **KV cache manager** and **GPU workers**.

- The **scheduler** picks which requests run in the next step and how many of their tokens.
- The **KV cache manager** owns the GPU memory that holds every request's keys and values (the *KV cache*) and says yes or no to each allocation. It cuts that memory into fixed-size **blocks**, each holding the keys and values of a fixed number of tokens (16 by default in vLLM), and keeps count of the **free** ones. Each request gets a **block table**: the list, in order, of the blocks that hold its tokens, so its cache need not sit in one piece. Lesson 5 shows why blocks beat one big chunk per request.
- The **model executor** (workers, one per GPU) runs the forward pass. It does not make policy decisions.

blocks.title: One request through one engine step

nodes.label:
KV cache manager
block pool, tables

scenes.caption: A prompt arrives over HTTP. The API server turns text into token ids; it never touches the GPU.
The request joins the scheduler's waiting queue. Nothing runs yet: the scheduler admits work only at step boundaries.
Before admitting it, the scheduler asks the KV cache manager whether enough free blocks exist for the prompt's keys and values. If not, the request keeps waiting.
The scheduler sends one control message per step: the token ids to process for every scheduled request plus each request's block table.
The workers run one forward pass for the whole batch. Attention reads earlier tokens' K and V from the blocks named in the tables and writes the new ones.
Each request's sampled token comes back to the scheduler, which appends it, checks stop conditions and hands text to the API server to stream.
When the request stops, the scheduler tells the KV cache manager to free its blocks, and the next step can admit someone else into that memory.

blocks.md:
The heart of the server is a loop the papers call an **iteration** or **step**: schedule, run one forward pass, process outputs, repeat. Orca's scheduler does exactly this: select requests, invoke the engine for one iteration, receive the generated tokens. vLLM's current architecture runs the scheduler and KV cache manager inside an **engine core** process with a busy loop, a separate **API server** process for HTTP and tokenization, and one **GPU worker** process per GPU.

Two latency numbers come out of this loop. **Time to first token (TTFT)** covers queueing plus the prefill step. **Inter-token latency (ITL)** is the gap between later tokens, roughly the duration of one step. Lesson 3 separates it from time per output token (TPOT), a request's average gap. Throughput is the total tokens produced per second across all requests.

Tensor parallelism splits each layer's attention heads across GPUs. Every shard still processes the same token positions, so the vLLM paper keeps a *single* KV cache manager in the scheduler: all workers use the same physical block ids, and each worker stores only the slice of K and V for its own heads. Per step, the scheduler broadcasts token ids and block tables; the workers synchronize activations among themselves with all-reduce and send sampled tokens back. **All-reduce** is a collective operation: every GPU contributes a tensor of the same shape, and every GPU ends up with their elementwise sum. It is needed because each GPU's heads produce only a partial result of the layer's output projection, and the sum of those partial results is the full output the next layer needs. The workers never negotiate memory with each other.

A forward pass is not the whole step. Around it the engine does CPU work: the scheduler picks requests and allocates blocks, **input preparation** builds the token ids, positions and block tables the kernels read, and **output processing** appends each sampled token, checks stop conditions and turns tokens back into text (**detokenization**). Launching each of the forward pass's many small kernels costs CPU time too. While the CPU is busy, the GPU waits.

This matters most when the GPU part is short. vLLM's V1 announcement notes that for small models on H100 GPUs the GPU time per step can be as low as about 5 ms, and SGLang's v0.4 post says an unoptimized engine can spend as much as half of its time on CPU overhead.

blocks.title: CPU work around two decode steps (illustrative durations)

scenes.caption: One process does everything. Illustrative numbers: a 5 ms forward pass with 2.5 ms of CPU work on each side. The GPU is idle half the time, the worst case SGLang describes.

Detokenizing and streaming move to a separate process (vLLM's API server, SGLang's detokenizer), so they overlap the next step. The engine core keeps only a short output update. Each step now takes 8.5 ms.
SGLang's scheduler runs one batch ahead: it prepares step 2 while the GPU runs step 1, using placeholders for tokens not sampled yet. The forward passes now run back to back, 5 ms per step.

blocks.md:
The figure shows two of the fixes. vLLM V1 runs the scheduler and executor in an isolated **engine core** loop while tokenization, detokenization and streaming happen in the API server process, and it keeps a **persistent batch**: the input tensors are cached and only the changes are applied each step, instead of rebuilding them. SGLang's scheduler since v0.4 runs one batch ahead and resolves the dependency on tokens not yet sampled with placeholder "future tokens".

The launch cost inside the forward pass needs a third fix. A **CUDA graph** records a step's kernel launches once and replays them with a single launch. A graph has fixed shapes, so vLLM captures graphs for a list of batch sizes and [pads each batch](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/config/compilation.py) up to the smallest captured size that holds it. The *CPU and GPU co-scheduling* course explains graphs, and the *vLLM attention backends* course how vLLM pads and splits them.

The scheduler decides **what** runs each step, the KV cache manager decides whether it **fits**, and the executor just runs a forward pass over token ids and block tables. Almost every serving optimization in this course is a change to the first two.

blocks.question: A model runs with tensor parallelism over 4 GPUs. Why can one KV cache manager in the scheduler hand the same block table to all 4 workers?
options: Each worker stores the whole KV cache, so memory is simply replicated 4 times
Every shard processes the same token positions and stores only its own heads' slice, so block ids mean the same thing on every GPU
Workers allocate blocks themselves and report back after every step
Block tables are only used on GPU 0, which forwards keys and values to the others
blocks.explain: Tensor parallelism splits heads, not positions. Block 17 holds positions 32 to 47 on every GPU, each GPU keeping the K and V of its own heads there. One mapping therefore serves all workers, which is why vLLM centralizes the manager.

blocks.question: A small model's forward pass takes 5 ms on the GPU, but at batch 1 the server emits a token only every 10 ms, and the GPU timeline shows gaps between steps. What helps most?
options: A GPU with twice the memory bandwidth
A larger max_num_batched_tokens
Overlapping the CPU's scheduling and output work with the GPU, and replaying the forward pass as a CUDA graph
Storing the KV cache in FP8
blocks.explain: The gaps are CPU time: scheduling, input preparation, output processing and kernel launches. More bandwidth or a smaller KV cache only shortens the 5 ms the GPU is already busy. Overlapping CPU work with the previous step and cutting launch cost removes the idle time itself.

blocks.question: A server is busy decoding 200 requests when a new request with a 3,000-token prompt arrives. Which latency number is this new request's prefill step most directly part of?
options: Its time to first token
Its inter-token latency
The throughput of the other requests only
None, prefill happens before the request is queued
blocks.explain: The first token can only be sampled after the prompt's keys and values exist, so queueing plus the prefill step make up TTFT. That same step can also slow the 200 running requests' next token, which is the tension the next lesson's token budget manages.

blocks.md:
Classic model servers schedule at **request granularity**: form a batch, run it until every request in it is done, then form the next one. Orca's paper names the two failures this causes for text generation. **Early-finished** requests keep occupying the batch (the engine even keeps computing for them) and cannot be returned until the slowest request ends. **Late-joining** requests must wait for the whole running batch to finish before they can start.

The GPU course showed the resulting timeline. Here we look at what a scheduler must do differently to fix it.

Orca's answer is **iteration-level scheduling**: the scheduler regains control after *every* forward pass. It repeats three things: select the requests to run next, invoke the engine for one iteration over them, and receive one output token per request. A finished request is returned at once, and a new request waits at most one iteration before it can be picked. This is what other systems call **continuous batching** or **in-flight batching** (the term used by TensorRT-LLM, NVIDIA's open-source library for LLM inference).

There is a catch. In one iteration some requests are decoding a single token while new ones are prefilling prompts of different lengths, so their inputs cannot be stacked into one rectangular `[B, L, H]` tensor (B requests, L tokens each, hidden size H). Orca's fix is **selective batching**: flatten all tokens of all requests into one `[sum of L, H]` matrix for the operations that do not care which request a token belongs to, and split by request only for attention.

blocks.title: Selective batching in Orca (one layer, simplified)

scenes.caption: Orca's example batch: x1 and x2 are decoding (1 new token each), x3 and x4 are new prompts with 2 and 3 tokens. Padding them into one [B, L, H] tensor is impossible, so all 7 tokens are flattened into [7, H].
Linear layers, LayerNorm, GeLU and residual adds treat every token independently, so they run once over the 7-row matrix. This is where batching pays: one weight read serves all 7 tokens.
Attention must only mix tokens of the same request, so a Split operation cuts the 7 rows back into per-request pieces.
Decoding requests also need keys and values of all their earlier tokens, which the K/V manager kept from previous iterations. Prompts attend among their own new tokens.
Merge stacks the outputs back into [7, H] and the following linear layers are batched again. The engine returns one sampled token per request.

blocks.tex: X \in \mathbb{R}^{\left(\sum_{i} L_i\right) \times H},\qquad L_i = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{request } i \text{ decoding} \\ \text{prompt length} & \text{request } i \text{ prefilling} \end{cases}
blocks.caption: The packed input of one step: one row per token, H columns. A decoding request adds 1 row, a prefilling request one row per prompt token it runs. Matrix multiplies and norms run over all rows at once; only attention needs the per-request boundaries.

blocks.md: Modern engines keep this design and make the step size explicit as a **token budget**. vLLM's current scheduler treats prompt and output tokens the same way: each step it builds a map from request id to number of tokens to compute, bounded by `max_num_batched_tokens` (tokens per step) and `max_num_seqs` (requests per step). With **chunked prefill**, enabled by default where possible, it schedules running requests first, so pending decodes always get their token, then fills the leftover budget with prefills, cutting a prompt into chunks if it does not fit. TensorRT-LLM exposes the same two limits as `max_batch_size` and `max_num_tokens`.

blocks.prompt: Budget 12 tokens, at most 4 requests. R1 and R2 arrive with 5-token prompts, R3 with a 7-token prompt. After R1 and R2 prefill in step 1, only 2 tokens of budget remain. What should happen to R3 in step 1?
blocks.reveal: Without chunking, R3 simply cannot run: 7 tokens do not fit in 2, so it waits a full step (TensorRT-LLM's documentation shows exactly this situation). With **chunked prefill**, R3 runs its first 2 prompt tokens now and the remaining 5 next step. Its KV cache for positions 0 and 1 is written in step 1 and reused in step 2, just like a decode reuses earlier tokens.

blocks.title: Packing a 12-token budget, at most 4 requests

scenes.caption: Step 1: R1 and R2 each prefill 5 prompt tokens. Only 2 tokens of budget remain, so the 7-token prompt of R3 is chunked: its first 2 tokens run now.
Step 2: running requests go first. R1 and R2 decode 1 token each, R3 finishes its last 5 prompt tokens, and R4's 4-token prompt fits. R5 waits: 4 requests is the sequence limit.
Step 3: four decodes use only 4 of 12 tokens. The budget is not the limit here, the sequence cap is. R1 emits its 3rd and last token and finishes.
Step 4: R1's slot was freed at the end of step 3, so R5's 9-token prompt joins the same step as three decodes: 12 tokens, a full budget.
Step 5: R2 and R3 finish. Requests left and joined at step boundaries, never waiting for a whole batch to drain.

blocks.md: The budget is a latency dial. vLLM's tuning guide says a smaller `max_num_batched_tokens` (for example 2048) gives better inter-token latency because fewer prefill tokens slow down each decode step, while a larger budget gives better time to first token because more prompt tokens are processed per step. Mixing the two kinds of work in one step also helps utilization: prefill tokens are compute-bound, decode tokens are memory-bound, so they use different resources of the same GPU pass.

Continuous batching does **not** mean padding requests to a common length. The tokens are packed with no padding, and only attention looks at per-request boundaries. TensorRT-LLM's in-flight batching explicitly requires packed (unpadded) inputs for this reason.
The scheduler's unit of work is a step with a token budget, not a request. Requests enter and leave between steps, and every step is a fresh decision about who gets how many tokens.

blocks.question: Budget 2048 tokens per step, chunked prefill on. 50 requests are decoding when a 6,000-token prompt arrives. What happens over the next few steps?
options: The 50 decodes pause until the 6,000-token prefill finishes in one large step
The prompt is rejected because it exceeds the token budget
Each step runs the 50 decode tokens first and spends the remaining 1,998 tokens on the next chunk of the prompt, so the prefill takes about 4 steps while decoding never stops
The prompt is split across 50 requests, one chunk each
blocks.explain: Decodes are scheduled first (1 token each), and the leftover budget goes to prefill chunks: 6,000 / 1,998 is a bit over 3, so 4 steps. Inter-token latency of the 50 stays bounded, and the new request's TTFT grows a little in exchange.

blocks.question: Why does selective batching split the batch for attention but not for the QKV projection?
options: Attention has no weights, so batching it gains nothing and it must be skipped
The QKV projection runs on the CPU
Splitting the projection would require padding, splitting attention does not
Each token's projection uses only that token's row, but attention must combine a token only with earlier tokens of its own request
blocks.explain: A linear layer computes each output row from one input row, so the request a row belongs to is irrelevant and all rows share one weight read. Attention mixes rows, and mixing rows from different requests would be wrong, so it needs the boundaries (and each request's own past keys and values).

lessons.title: Measuring a server: latency percentiles, load curves and benchmarks

blocks.md:
Lesson 1 named two latencies, TTFT and ITL, and lesson 2 claimed a token budget trades one for the other. To check claims like that, or to tune your own server, you need to measure them the way users feel them.

Start with one request, using made-up timestamps. It arrives at 0 ms, waits 40 ms in the queue and prefills for 60 ms, so its first token appears at 100 ms. Its next five tokens arrive at 110, 120, 230, 240 and 250 ms. The 110 ms gap happened because another request's long prompt was prefilled in the same step.

scenes.caption: The request waits 40 ms for a step with room for it, then its prompt is prefilled. The first token is sampled at 100 ms: its time to first token.
Tokens 2 and 3 come one decode step apart, 10 ms each.
Token 4 takes 110 ms: the step that produced it also ran another request's prompt chunk. Nothing about this request changed, yet the user sees the stream freeze.
Tokens 5 and 6 are back to 10 ms. End-to-end latency is 250 ms for 6 tokens.

blocks.md:
Four numbers describe this one request:

- **TTFT**: first token time minus arrival, 100 ms. It includes queueing and prefill (and the network, seen from a real client).
- **ITL** (inter-token latency): every gap between consecutive tokens, here 10, 10, 110, 10 and 10 ms. A request with $n$ tokens contributes $n - 1$ gaps.
- **TPOT** (time per output token): the request's average gap, (end-to-end latency minus TTFT) / (tokens minus 1), here (250 minus 100) / 5 = 30 ms.
- **End-to-end latency**: 250 ms.

`vllm bench serve` computes TPOT per request with exactly that formula and collects ITL as every gap. Names differ between tools: NVIDIA's benchmarking guide, like the GPU course, calls the averaged number ITL and says it is also known as TPOT. Check which one a report means.

Over a whole run these become distributions. Per-request numbers (TTFT, TPOT, end-to-end) give one sample per request; ITL gives one sample per gap. You report **percentiles**: p50 (the median), p90, p99 (99% of samples are at or below it). Throughput numbers are totals over the run: output tokens per second and requests per second, each divided by the time from the first request to the last response.

blocks.prompt: In the example, the median ITL is 10 ms and the TPOT is 30 ms. Neither shows what the user actually experienced at token 4. Which statistic over many requests would?
blocks.reveal: A high percentile of ITL (p99, or the maximum). TPOT spreads the 110 ms freeze evenly over 5 gaps, so it looks like a steady 30 ms stream; the median ignores the freeze entirely. Over a whole benchmark, stalls like this sit in the tail of the ITL distribution, which is why benchmark tools report ITL percentiles separately from TPOT.

blocks.md:
A server has no single latency: it depends on the load you offer. To see this, sweep the **request rate** and measure at each rate. Arrivals should be random, like real users: a **Poisson process** sends requests independently at a fixed average rate, which is what `vllm bench serve --request-rate` generates by default.

The figure comes from a toy simulation (script-computed, not measured): Llama 3 8B on one A100-80GB with the GPU course's peak-rate step model plus attention FLOPs and KV reads, decodes scheduled first, chunked prefill, prompts of 200 to 3,800 tokens and outputs of 50 to 350 tokens, 1,500 requests per rate with the first 10% dropped as warm-up. Simplified: admission reserves each request's true prompt plus output length in a 52 GB KV pool, so nothing is ever preempted. Each prefill chunk is charged 128 tokens of extra compute, which matches the overhead of up to about 25% that Sarathi-Serve measured for 512-token chunks on Yi-34B (and is small at 2,048).

blocks.title: p99 latency vs load for three token budgets (toy simulation)

scenes.caption: 2 requests per second, light load. ITL p99 already depends on the budget: a step that carries a 2,048 or 8,192-token prefill chunk stalls every decode in it. The small budget has the worst TTFT, because each prompt needs more, less efficient steps.
4 requests per second. TTFT tails grow with queueing. The 8,192 budget lets several prompts share one huge step, so its ITL p99 climbs to about 200 ms.

6 requests per second, near capacity. This model charges budget 512 25% extra compute on every prefill chunk, so it is closest to saturation and its TTFT p99 is almost twice budget 2,048's. Budget 8,192's ITL p99 reaches 449 ms.

7 requests per second. Budget 512 is past its capacity (about 6.4 requests per second in this model): its queue grows for as long as the test runs, so its TTFT p99 is about 20 s and would keep rising in a longer test.

blocks.md: Three lessons from the sweep. First, the simulation reproduces lesson 2's trade: the small budget gives the best ITL and the worst TTFT. Second, all three configurations deliver the same tokens per second until they saturate, because below capacity throughput simply equals the offered load; a throughput number alone cannot tell them apart. Third, latency rises slowly and then very fast near capacity. Why queues explode near full utilization, and how to read percentiles under load, is the subject of the *Tail latency* course.

blocks.caption: Little's law: the average number of requests in the system (L) equals the arrival rate (lambda) times the average time each spends in it (W). It holds for any stable system, whatever the scheduler.

blocks.md:
Worked number: with budget 2,048 at 5 requests per second, the simulation's mean end-to-end latency is 5.24 s, so on average $5 \times 5.24 \approx 26$ requests are in the server, and the simulation's own time-average count was 26.5.

Little's law explains why two benchmark styles disagree. An **open-loop** benchmark fixes the rate $\lambda$ and lets concurrency follow. A **closed-loop** one fixes concurrency (in `vllm bench serve`, `--max-concurrency` with the default unlimited `--request-rate`): each client sends its next request only after the last one returns, so when the server slows down, the rate drops with it and the queue never builds. Real users arrive whether or not you are slow, so latency at a fixed rate is the number to trust; the *Tail latency* course shows how closed-loop testers hide stalls (coordinated omission).

Throughput also counts requests that were too slow to be useful. **Goodput** counts only the requests that meet every latency target, or **SLO** (service level objective), such as TTFT under 1 s and TPOT under 50 ms. `vllm bench serve --goodput ttft:1000 tpot:50` adds a request goodput line: requests per second that met all the given limits, in milliseconds. DistServe, the subject of the *Disaggregated prefill and decode* course, defines goodput a little differently: the highest request rate at which a target share (say 90%) of requests meets the SLOs.

# not run here: needs an NVIDIA GPU
vllm serve meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct --max-num-batched-tokens 2048

# in another shell; repeat for several --request-rate values
vllm bench serve --model meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct \
  --dataset-name random --random-input-len 2000 --random-output-len 200 \
  --ignore-eos --num-prompts 1000 --request-rate 4 \
  --percentile-metrics ttft,tpot,itl,e2el --metric-percentiles 50,90,99 \
  --goodput ttft:1000 tpot:50
blocks.caption: Not run here (no NVIDIA GPU on this machine). It prints request throughput, request goodput and output token throughput, then mean, median and the chosen percentiles of TTFT, TPOT, ITL and end-to-end latency. --ignore-eos makes every request generate all 200 tokens.

blocks.md: Common benchmarking mistakes: measuring at one rate (or at concurrency 1) and calling it the server's latency; no warm-up; repeated prompts that hit the prefix cache and make TTFT look tiny; output lengths unlike production (too short flatters everything); reporting means without p99; comparing runs with different prompt or output lengths.

A serving benchmark is a curve, not a number: sweep the request rate with random arrivals, and at each rate report p50 and p99 of TTFT, TPOT and ITL plus goodput under your SLOs. Throughput equals offered load until saturation, so the interesting part is where latency bends.

blocks.question: A benchmark at concurrency 1 shows 9 ms ITL and 150 ms TTFT. The server is then put behind an API that receives 200 requests per second, about 30 times what the earlier load sweep showed it can sustain. What will users see?
options: The same 9 ms ITL and 150 ms TTFT, since continuous batching adds requests for free
Lower latency, because larger batches use the GPU more efficiently
The server rejects the extra requests automatically and the accepted ones keep 9 ms ITL
A queue that grows for as long as the overload lasts: TTFT grows without bound, and ITL rises as steps fill with prefill chunks and larger batches
blocks.explain: Above capacity, arrivals exceed completions, so the waiting queue and TTFT grow with time (Little's law with an ever-growing W). Steps also fill up with prompt chunks and more sequences, so ITL rises. A concurrency-1 run measures the empty server, not the loaded one.

blocks.question: Two configurations have the same mean TPOT, 30 ms. Configuration X has a p99 ITL of 40 ms, configuration Y of 450 ms. Which statement is most likely?
options: Y uses a larger token budget, so some steps carry big prefill chunks that stall every decode in them
X uses a larger token budget
Y has a smaller KV pool
The two are equivalent for users, since TPOT is the same
blocks.explain: Equal averages with very different tails point to occasional long steps. A large budget lets a step carry thousands of prompt tokens, and every decoding request in that step waits for it. TPOT averages those stalls away; the ITL tail shows them.

lessons.title: KV cache accounting: from bytes per token to batch size

blocks.md: Every serving decision in lesson 2 silently assumed the answer to one question: does this request's KV cache fit? To answer it the scheduler needs exact accounting. Each layer stores one key vector and one value vector per **KV head** for every token. With **grouped-query attention (GQA)**, several query heads share one KV head, so the number of KV heads $n_{kv}$ can be much smaller than the number of query heads. Each key or value vector has $d_{\text{head}}$ numbers (the head dimension), and each number takes $b$ bytes. So one token costs 2 vectors (K and V) times the number of layers times $n_{kv}$ times $d_{\text{head}}$ numbers times $b$ bytes.

The value of $b$ comes from the number format. **FP16** (half precision) splits its 16 bits into 1 sign bit, 5 exponent bits and 10 mantissa bits. **BF16**, the "brain floating point" format from Google Brain, is also 16 bits but splits them as 1 sign, 8 exponent and 7 mantissa bits, so it covers the same range as a 32-bit float with less precision. **FP8** squeezes a float into 8 bits, for example 1 sign, 4 exponent and 3 mantissa bits. For memory only the width matters: 16 bits is 2 bytes, 8 bits is 1 byte.

blocks.tex: \text{bytes per token} = 2 \times n_{\text{layers}} \times n_{kv} \times d_{\text{head}} \times b
blocks.caption: 2 for K and V; b is bytes per value (2 for FP16 or BF16, 1 for FP8).

blocks.md:
Worked example: **Llama 3 8B**. The Llama 3 paper lists 32 layers, model dimension 4,096, 32 attention heads and 8 key/value heads, so $d_{\text{head}} = 4096/32 = 128$. In BF16:

$2 \times 32 \times 8 \times 128 \times 2 = 131{,}072$ bytes, exactly **128 KiB per token**.

The GPU course found 512 KiB per token for LLaMA-7B, which has a similar size but one KV head per query head. GQA with 8 KV heads instead of 32 cuts this by 32 over 8, which is 4x. A full 8,192-token context still costs $8192 \times 128$ KiB $= 1$ GiB, and Llama 3 70B (80 layers, also 8 KV heads) needs 320 KiB per token.

Next, how much memory is there for KV? Engines decide this once at startup. vLLM loads the weights, runs a profiling pass to measure peak activation memory (the temporary tensors a forward pass creates), and turns the rest of its allowance into KV blocks. The allowance is `gpu_memory_utilization`, a fraction of GPU memory; recent releases on CUDA and ROCm default it to 1.0 and size the pool from the memory actually free after warmup, other platforms to 0.92. The profiling pass uses a dummy step of [`max_num_batched_tokens` tokens](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/v1/worker/gpu/model_runner.py), the largest step the scheduler may build, so raising the token budget raises the measured peak and shrinks the KV pool. TensorRT-LLM's `free_gpu_memory_fraction` (default 0.9) is the share of *free* GPU memory given to the KV cache. Worked numbers below assume an 80 GB GPU (80 x 10^9 bytes), a 0.9 fraction of the whole GPU, and 4 GB of activations.

blocks.title: How an 80 GB GPU is carved up at startup (Llama 3 8B)

scenes.caption: The engine may use 90% of 80 GB, which is 72 GB, so 8 GB is left alone. Loading 8 billion BF16 parameters at 2 bytes each takes 16 GB.
A profiling forward pass with a dummy step of max_num_batched_tokens tokens measures peak activation and workspace memory. We assume 4 GB here.
Everything left becomes one pool of KV blocks, allocated once up front: 72 minus 16 minus 4 leaves 52 GB. This number, not compute, will cap how many requests can run.
Raise max_num_batched_tokens and the dummy step grows with it. If the peak became 8 GB (an assumed figure), the pool would shrink to 48 GB: 366,210 token slots instead of 396,728, about 8% fewer.

blocks.caption: The pool for our example: 52 billion bytes divided by 131,072 bytes per token gives 396,728 token slots (rounded down), and dividing by 16 tokens per block (vLLM's default block size) gives 24,795 blocks.

blocks.md: Now the batch size. If each request reserves its full 8,192-token context, only $\lfloor 396{,}728 / 8192 \rfloor = 48$ requests fit, no matter how short they turn out to be. If each request holds only the blocks it actually uses, a 1,500-token sequence needs $\lceil 1500/16 \rceil = 94$ blocks (1,504 slots) and $\lfloor 24{,}795 / 94 \rfloor = 263$ of them fit. That is 5.5x more sequences to share each weight read, from bookkeeping alone.

blocks.title: How many sequences fit in the KV pool

scenes.caption: Llama 3 8B, 128 KiB per token, 52 GB pool. Reserving the full 8,192-token context per request caps the batch at 48. Allocating only what is used fits 263 sequences of 1,500 tokens.
Same pool with 512 KiB per token (a model with full multi-head attention, like LLaMA-7B). Every curve drops 4x: GQA's smaller KV directly multiplies the batch size.
An FP8 KV cache stores 1 byte per value, halving the per-token size to 64 KiB, so twice as many sequences fit at every length.
Shrinking the pool to 20 GB (say, a bigger model on the same GPU) scales every curve down proportionally. Both knobs act the same way: capacity is pool size divided by bytes per token.

blocks.md: Model weights are paid once; KV is paid per token per sequence. A common mistake is to size a deployment by "the model fits on the GPU". A model that fits with 2 GB to spare can serve almost nobody: 2 GB is only about 15,000 tokens of Llama 3 8B's KV cache.

Capacity in sequences is roughly pool bytes / (bytes per token x tokens per sequence). Every lever (GQA, FP8 KV, more GPUs, smaller weights, shorter contexts, less waste per sequence) moves one of those three terms.

Everything so far assumed every layer is full attention with the same per-token cost. Newer models break that in three ways.

- **Sliding-window layers** attend only to the last $W$ tokens, so such a layer's cache stops growing at about $W$ tokens per sequence. OpenAI's gpt-oss models alternate sliding-window layers ($W = 128$) with full-attention layers.
- **Multi-head latent attention (MLA)**, used by DeepSeek-V2 and V3, caches one compressed latent per token per layer instead of per-head keys and values: 576 numbers per layer in DeepSeek-V3 (a 512-number latent plus a 64-number positional key), so its 61 layers cost $61 \times 576 \times 2 = 70{,}272$ bytes per token in BF16. The *Multi-head latent attention* course derives it.
- **State-space (Mamba) layers** keep one fixed-size state per sequence, however long it gets. The *Hybrid attention and SSM models* course counts those bytes.

One allocator has to serve all of these. vLLM's **hybrid KV cache manager** keeps a single pool of equal-size pages and splits the layers into **KV cache groups**: every layer in a group has the same attention type, and every group has the same page size. A request gets separate block tables per group, and sliding-window groups free their blocks as tokens fall out of the window.

The design doc's example: 10 full-attention layers and 20 sliding-window layers (window 32) become three groups of 10, and a 112-token request with block size 16 holds 11 blocks: 7 for the full group and 2 for each sliding group. Mamba layers fit by raising the attention block size until a page is as large as one layer's state and padding the state to that size.

blocks.caption: gpt-oss-120b in BF16: 36 layers alternating sliding-window (window 128) and full attention, 8 KV heads of dimension 64, so 2 x 8 x 64 x 2 = 2,048 bytes (2 KiB) per token per layer. The sliding term ignores rounding up to whole blocks.

blocks.md: If all 36 layers were full attention, the same sequence would need $8192 \times 36 \times 2$ KiB $= 576$ MiB. The window cuts it almost in half, and the saving approaches exactly half as sequences grow, because only the 18 full layers keep growing. In a 20 GB pool (an assumed figure), $\lfloor 20 \times 10^9 / (292.5 \times 2^{20}) \rfloor = 65$ such sequences fit instead of 33, but only if the allocator really frees the out-of-window blocks; one that sizes every layer like a full-attention layer gets the 33.

blocks.question: Llama 3 70B has 80 layers, 64 query heads, 8 KV heads and head dimension 128. What is its BF16 KV cache per token?
options: 160 KiB
2.5 MiB
320 KiB
640 KiB
blocks.explain: 2 x 80 x 8 x 128 x 2 = 327,680 bytes = 320 KiB. Using the 64 query heads instead of the 8 KV heads gives 2.5 MiB (the GQA mistake); dropping the factor 2 for K and V gives 160 KiB; using 4-byte values gives 640 KiB.

blocks.question: All requests are about 2,000 tokens long and memory-bound by KV. Which single change roughly doubles the number of sequences that fit?
options: Storing the KV cache in FP8 instead of BF16
Doubling max_num_seqs
Doubling the block size from 16 to 32
Enabling chunked prefill
blocks.explain: FP8 halves b in the formula, so twice as many tokens fit in the same pool. Raising max_num_seqs only lifts a cap that is not binding; block size changes waste per sequence by a few tokens; chunked prefill changes step composition, not memory per token.

blocks.question: A model has 24 full-attention layers and 24 sliding-window layers (window 1,024), all with the same KV bytes per token per layer. For 32,768-token sequences, roughly what fraction of an all-full-attention model's KV cache does it need?
options: About 1/48
About 3/4
The same, because sliding-window layers still store every token
About 1/2
blocks.explain: Full layers store 32,768 tokens each, sliding layers about 1,024: (24 x 32,768 + 24 x 1,024) / (48 x 32,768) = 0.516. The full-attention half dominates at long context, so the cache is about half, and only if the allocator frees blocks outside the window.

lessons.title: Fragmentation, and block tables as page tables

blocks.md:
Why did older servers reserve the maximum length? Most deep learning frameworks want each tensor in one contiguous piece of memory, so systems like FasterTransformer (NVIDIA's earlier transformer inference library) and Orca stored each request's KV cache as one contiguous chunk sized for the longest output it might produce. The vLLM paper names three resulting kinds of waste:

- **Reserved**: slots that will hold this request's future tokens, but sit empty for most of its life.
- **Internal fragmentation**: slots past the point where the request actually stopped, never used.
- **External fragmentation**: free memory between chunks that is too small for the next request.

It measured only 20.4% to 38.2% of KV memory holding real token states in those systems.

To see the mechanism with numbers you can trace, the bars below come from a toy simulation (script-computed, not from a paper). The contiguous policy places each reservation by **first-fit**: scan the pool from the start and take the first free gap big enough for it. Pool: 65,536 token slots, which is 8 GiB at Llama 3 8B's 128 KiB per token. Workload: 20,000 queued requests with prompts of 64 to 1,024 tokens, a client-set maximum length of 512, 1,024 or 2,048 tokens, and exponentially distributed outputs averaging 300 tokens before the cap. One token per running request per step, 4,000 steps, measured after a 500-step warmup.

blocks.title: Where the KV pool goes: toy simulation, 8 GiB pool

scenes.caption: Contiguous, first-fit, each request reserves its client-set maximum length (512, 1024 or 2048). Only 41% of the pool holds real tokens; a third is never-to-be-used tail space.
Paged, block size 16, blocks allocated when needed. 98.4% holds real tokens. Nothing is reserved ahead, and the only internal waste is the unfilled tail of each sequence's last block (1.1%).
Paged with block size 128. Same scheme, but each last block wastes up to 127 slots, so internal fragmentation grows to 8.2% and real tokens fall to 91.3%.

blocks.md: Paging fixes all three wastes at once, the same way an operating system does. Memory is cut into equal **physical blocks** (vLLM's default is 16 tokens). A request owns a list of **logical blocks** filled left to right, and its **block table** maps each logical block to whichever physical block it got. A new block is allocated only when the last one is full, so nothing is reserved ahead, internal waste is at most one partly filled block per sequence (on average about half a block: $B/2$ tokens for block size $B$, roughly 8 tokens at size 16, because a sequence is about equally likely to end anywhere inside its last block), and since every block is the same size, any free block fits any request: no external fragmentation.

blocks.title: Virtual memory concepts, mapped to the KV cache

scenes.caption: The vLLM paper's analogy: a request is a process and its tokens are the bytes of its address space.
The KV cache is split into fixed-size blocks, like pages. Logical blocks are filled left to right as tokens arrive.
Each request has a block table mapping logical to physical blocks. There is no MMU or TLB: the attention kernel reads the table itself and computes addresses in software.
Physical blocks are interchangeable, so any free block can back any logical block. Equal sizes mean no external fragmentation.
When memory runs out, an OS swaps pages to disk. The KV manager can swap blocks to CPU memory, or throw them away and recompute them, an option an OS does not have.

blocks.md: For the scheduler, paging turns memory accounting into integer arithmetic. Instead of searching for a large enough hole, "does it fit?" becomes "is the number of blocks this request needs at most the number of free blocks?".

blocks.title: The manager's view: block tables and a free count (block size 4)

scenes.caption: Prefill: A (6-token prompt) gets blocks 0 and 1; B (3 tokens) gets block 2. The manager only needs a count of free blocks to admit them: 5 left.
Two decode steps later A holds 8 tokens (block 1 now full) and B holds 5, so B's 5th token needed a new block: block 3. Free count 4.

C arrives with a 9-token prompt, needing ceil(9/4) = 3 blocks. 3 is at most 4, so it is admitted into blocks 4, 5, 6. Admission needed only a count of free blocks, not a search for a large enough hole.

A's 9th token crosses a block boundary and takes the last free block, 7, so A's blocks 0, 1, 7 are no longer contiguous, which is fine. The pool is now full; the next block request will need a policy (next lesson).
B finishes. Its blocks 2 and 3 return to the free pool immediately and can be reused by anyone, in any order. No compaction, no searching for a large enough hole.

blocks.md: The analogy is not exact, and the differences matter. The OS translates every memory access in hardware; here the attention kernel is rewritten to fetch keys and values block by block through the table (the PagedAttention course covers that kernel, block sharing and prefix caching in depth). **Prefix caching** means a new request reuses the KV blocks an earlier request already computed for the same opening tokens, so its prefill skips them. For example, if two chat requests start with the same 1,024-token system prompt and the block size is 16, the second finds the prompt's 64 full blocks already computed, points its block table at them and prefills only its own question. An OS evicts individual pages by predicted reuse; a sequence needs *all* its blocks every step, so vLLM evicts all or nothing per sequence. And an OS cannot recreate a page it threw away, while a KV block can always be recomputed from the tokens.

Paging does not shrink the KV cache. A 1,500-token sequence still needs 1,500 tokens of K and V. Paging removes the memory that held *nothing*, which is why the gain is largest when requests are short relative to their maximum length.
Fixed-size blocks plus a per-request table make KV memory behave like virtual memory: allocate on demand, any block fits anywhere, and waste is bounded by one partial block per sequence.

blocks.question: In the contiguous simulation, 12.8% of the pool was free yet the next request in line could not start. Which kind of waste is this?
options: Internal fragmentation
Reserved slots
Activation memory
External fragmentation
blocks.explain: Free memory existed, but not as one contiguous run long enough for the waiting request's reservation. That is external fragmentation. With fixed-size blocks any free block is usable, so external fragmentation disappears; the 0.5% left free in the paged run is just too few blocks for the next prompt.

blocks.question: Paging lets a server admit a request after allocating only its prompt's blocks. What new problem does this create that max-length reservation did not have?
options: Requests can no longer share a batch
The pool can run out in the middle of generation, when running requests need new blocks that are not there
Prompts longer than one block cannot be stored
Block tables use more memory than the KV cache itself
blocks.explain: Reservation guaranteed every admitted request could finish. Allocating on demand bets that not everyone will grow at once; when the bet loses, some running request has nowhere to put its next token. Handling that is the job of preemption, the next lesson.

lessons.title: When the pool runs dry: admission control and preemption

blocks.md: A KV cache only grows, and nobody knows how long any request will run. Every scheduler therefore needs a rule for **admission control** (when to start a new request) and, unless that rule is very cautious, a rule for **preemption** (what to do when running requests outgrow memory).

Orca chose caution. When a request is scheduled for the first time, the scheduler reserves its `max_tokens` (the most tokens it can ever have) out of `n_slots`, the total number of KV slots the operator configured. If the reservation does not fit, the request waits. The paper explains why: without it, the scheduler can deadlock, unable to run any request because there is no room for anyone's next key and value.

blocks.caption: The admission part of Orca's Algorithm 1, rewritten in Python. A request's slots are released when it finishes.

blocks.md: vLLM bets the other way: allocate blocks only as tokens arrive, and handle the rare case when the pool runs out. Its paper fixes three rules. Scheduling is **first come, first served** (FCFS), and when it must preempt it evicts the **latest arrivals first**, so early requests are not starved. Eviction is **all or nothing** per sequence, because a sequence needs all of its blocks every step. And sequences of one request (say, the candidate outputs of beam search, which keeps the k most likely partial outputs alive and extends each by one token per step, or the n samples of parallel sampling) are **gang-scheduled**: preempted and resumed together. The paper also says that while preempted sequences are pending, no new requests are accepted.

blocks.title: A preemption step (simplified from vLLM's scheduler)
blocks.code:
def schedule(running, waiting, pool):
    preempted = []
    i = 0
    while i < len(running):              # oldest request first
        req = running[i]
        need = pool.blocks_needed(req)   # 0 or 1 block this step
        while need > pool.num_free and running[-1] is not req:
            victim = running.pop()       # latest arrival loses
            pool.free_all(victim)        # all or nothing
            victim.num_computed = 0      # its KV will be recomputed
            waiting.appendleft(victim)   # first in line to resume
            preempted.append(victim.id)
        if need > pool.num_free:         # nobody left to evict
            running.pop(i); pool.free_all(req)
            req.num_computed = 0
            waiting.appendleft(req); preempted.append(req.id)
            break
        pool.allocate(req, need)
        i += 1
    if not preempted:
        admit(waiting, running, pool)    # FCFS while blocks remain
    return preempted

scenes.caption: Running requests in arrival order: A, B, C. One free block. A's next token crosses a block boundary, so it needs 1 block.
A fits: it takes the last free block.
B also crosses a boundary and needs 1 block, but none are free.
The latest arrival, C, is the victim. All 3 of its blocks are freed at once, and its progress counter is reset because its KV is gone.
C goes to the front of the waiting queue, so it is the first to resume when memory frees up.
B now gets its block. The loop ends: A and B both decode this step.
A preemption happened, so no new request is admitted this step even though 2 blocks are free. Admitting one now would only invite the next preemption.
scenes.output:
preempted: ['C']
C later re-runs its prompt plus already generated tokens as one prefill.

blocks.md:
What happens to an evicted sequence's KV? The vLLM paper offers two recovery methods.

- **Swapping**: copy the blocks to CPU memory, managed by a separate CPU block allocator, and copy them back on resume. Swap space never needs to exceed the GPU's KV pool.
- **Recomputation**: drop the blocks. On resume, the prompt plus the tokens already generated become one longer prompt, rebuilt in a single prefill step, which is much faster than regenerating them one by one.

Its ablation (an experiment that changes one design choice and measures the effect) found that swapping suffers with small blocks, because many small CPU-GPU transfers waste bandwidth, while recompute cost does not depend on block size. Recompute wins with small blocks, swap with large ones, and for 16 to 64 they performed comparably.

blocks.title: Restoring a preempted sequence: a first-order cost model

scenes.caption: Llama 3 8B, 20 GB/s effective transfer, 200 TFLOP/s effective compute. Swapping moves 256 KiB per token (out and back) in about 13 us; recomputing costs 2N FLOPs per token (N = 8 billion parameters), about 80 us. Swap looks cheaper here.
Small blocks mean many small copies, and the vLLM paper found these cannot use the link's full bandwidth. At 3 GB/s effective, swap costs more than recompute.
A 13B model with full multi-head attention stores 800 KiB per token. Both costs rise, and at 20 GB/s swap is still cheaper on paper: the answer depends on the model's KV size per FLOP.

blocks.md: The plot charges a recompute only for the preempted request's own FLOPs, as if the GPU had nothing else to do. In a busy server those FLOPs come out of the shared token budget. With a 2,048-token budget and 48 running decodes, 2,000 tokens per step are left for prefill. A preempted request that resumes with 3,000 tokens (prompt plus generated) takes all of that for one step and half of the next, and every waiting prompt is pushed back by the same amount. The true cost of a recompute is spread over everyone else's TTFT (simplified: with prefix caching on, vLLM can reuse any of the victim's freed full blocks that were not reallocated yet); the *KV cache offloading* course makes the same busy-GPU argument for reloading versus recomputing cached prefixes.

blocks.title: Where a 2,048-token budget goes after a preemption

scenes.caption: No preemption: 48 decodes take 1 token each and 2,000 tokens of prefill go to new prompts every step.
Step 1 after the resume: the preempted request is first in the waiting queue, so its 3,000-token recompute takes all 2,000 prefill tokens. New prompts get nothing.
Step 2: the last 1,000 recomputed tokens, then 1,000 for new prompts. Over two steps, 3,000 tokens of prefill capacity, one and a half steps' worth, went to redoing old work.
Step 3: back to normal. The decodes never stopped, but every waiting prompt's TTFT grew by about one and a half steps.

blocks.md: Current vLLM makes the choice for you: its docs say that in V1 (the rewritten engine architecture from lesson 1) the default preemption mode is recompute, because recomputation has lower overhead in that architecture, and CPU swapping for preemption has been removed. If preemption happens often, the docs recommend more KV memory (`gpu_memory_utilization`, more tensor or pipeline parallelism) or fewer concurrent tokens (`max_num_seqs`, `max_num_batched_tokens`). **Pipeline parallelism** gives each GPU a different contiguous group of layers. Like tensor parallelism, it spreads the weights over more GPUs, which leaves each GPU more memory for KV.

The other engines sit between the two extremes. **TensorRT-LLM** makes it a setting: its default capacity policy `GUARANTEED_NO_EVICT` admits a request only if the blocks it needs *to completion* can be reserved, so a started request is never paused. `MAX_UTILIZATION` packs as many requests as possible and may pause some when KV runs out.

**SGLang**, another open-source serving engine, estimates instead of reserving every worst case: a new request is budgeted for its prompt plus its `max_new_tokens` (the client's cap on generated tokens, clipped at 4,096), but requests already running count only their remaining `max_new_tokens` times a *new token ratio*, its guess of what fraction of those tokens will really be generated. The ratio starts at a cautious 0.7 and decays every decode step toward a much smaller floor, so admission grows more optimistic over time. When decoding runs out of memory, it **retracts** some running requests back to the queue and resets the ratio from how much the remaining requests have actually generated.

blocks.title: Admission policy vs outcome (same toy simulation)

scenes.caption: Average number of running sequences. Reserving the worst case in blocks (no fragmentation) helps a little; allocating on demand more than doubles the batch.
Requests finished in 4,000 steps, assuming every step takes the same time. On-demand allocation finishes about 2.1x more than paged reservation.
Preemptions. Both reserving policies never preempt. On demand preempted 420 times and had to recompute about 230,000 prompt tokens, a cost this simplified model does not charge.

blocks.md: Preemption is not free throughput. The optimistic policy's extra batch size is partly spent redoing prefills, and a preempted request's latency can jump by a full prefill plus queueing. Frequent preemption is a sign the pool is too small for the configured concurrency.

Admission control is a bet about future output lengths. Reserve the worst case and you never preempt but waste memory; allocate on demand and you fit far more requests but need a preemption policy (latest arrival first, all of its blocks) and a recovery method (swap or recompute).

blocks.question: A service promises customers that a started response will never stall mid-stream, even at the cost of throughput. Which TensorRT-LLM capacity policy fits?
options: MAX_UTILIZATION
STATIC_BATCH
GUARANTEED_NO_EVICT
Any of them, since in-flight batching never pauses requests
blocks.explain: GUARANTEED_NO_EVICT reserves the blocks each request needs to finish before starting it, so started requests are never paused. MAX_UTILIZATION trades that guarantee for more concurrency. STATIC_BATCH is a legacy mode the docs advise against for production.

blocks.question: Why does vLLM preempt the latest-arrived request rather than the one holding the most blocks?
options: The latest request always holds the fewest blocks, so it is cheapest
First come, first served: evicting latecomers protects older requests from repeated preemption and starvation
Older requests cannot be preempted because their blocks are shared
The CPU swap space only accepts recent blocks
blocks.explain: The paper adopts FCFS for fairness and to prevent starvation, so early arrivals are served first and the latest are preempted first. Evicting the biggest request would free more memory but could evict the same long request again and again.

blocks.question: Spot the bug: a scheduler allocates blocks on demand, admits a new request whenever its prompt's blocks are free, and has no preemption code. What eventually happens under heavy load?
options: Running requests need new blocks that are not there, so the step cannot proceed: an out-of-memory failure or a deadlock
Nothing, block allocation can never fail
Throughput drops but every request still finishes
Requests are silently truncated to their prompt length and returned
blocks.explain: On-demand allocation without a fallback is exactly the deadlock Orca's reservation avoids: every running request may need one more block at the same moment. You need either worst-case reservation or preemption with swap or recompute.

lessons.title: Who goes next: priority, fairness and length-aware scheduling

blocks.md:
Lessons 4 to 6 answered one question: does a request fit? The scheduler has a second job: among the requests that could run, which goes first. Every engine so far used **first come, first served** (FCFS).

A tiny example shows where FCFS hurts. A batch job submits 4 requests that will each generate 4,000 tokens, a moment before 20 chat requests that will each generate 50. The server runs at most 4 sequences at once, and each running sequence gets one token per step (prefill ignored to keep the count simple).

blocks.prompt: Under FCFS the 4 long requests take all 4 slots first. When does the average chat request finish, and what if the server ran the shortest jobs first instead?
blocks.reveal: FCFS: the chat requests cannot start until step 4,000, finishing on average at step **4,150**; the mean over all 24 requests is 4,125 steps. Shortest job first (SJF): the chat requests run in 5 waves of 4 and finish on average at step **150**, and the long ones finish at 4,250 instead of 4,000, 6% later. The mean over all 24 drops to 833 steps. At Llama 3 8B's decode floor on an A100, about 7.85 ms per step (16 GB of BF16 weights read at 2.039 TB/s), that is roughly 33 s versus 1.2 s for a chat reply (script-computed).

blocks.title: Run order for 4 long and 20 short requests, 4 slots

scenes.caption: FCFS: arrival order. The four 4,000-token requests fill all 4 slots, and the first chat request starts only at step 4,000. This is **head-of-line blocking**: a long job at the front delays everything behind it.
SJF: shortest first. The 20 chat requests run in 5 waves and finish by step 250; only then do the long jobs start. Mean completion falls from 4,125 to 833 steps.

But the server does not know output lengths in advance. A length-aware scheduler must predict them, and a mistake (here S7 predicted long) only moves that request later; the order is still far better than FCFS.

blocks.md: SJF minimizes mean waiting time, but it needs each request's output length, which nobody knows until it stops. Fu et al. (2024) observe that exact lengths are hard to predict, but the *relative order* of lengths within a batch can be predicted, and order is all SJF needs. They append a linear layer to a small OPT language model (OPT-125M for a Llama-3-8B target, OPT-350M for 70B), so it outputs one score per prompt, and train it with **ListMLE**, a ranking loss that rewards putting a whole list in the right order. They measure success with **Kendall's tau**, a rank correlation: 1 means the predicted order matches the true order, 0 means no relation (FCFS order, for example, is unrelated to output length). Their vLLM-based scheduler reported 2.8x lower latency in chatbot serving and 6.5x higher throughput in synthetic data generation.

Pure SJF has a classic failure: **starvation**. If short requests keep arriving, a long one can wait forever. Fu et al.'s scheduler counts how many steps each waiting request was passed over; at a threshold (`StarvationThreshold`) the request is promoted to priority for a fixed number of steps (`PriorityQuantum`), then demoted again. They judge fairness per request by the longest a user waits between tokens, `max(TTFT, max TPOT)`.

A shared API raises a different question: fairness between **clients**. Rate limits (requests per minute) stop one customer from flooding the queue, but they also turn work away when the GPU is idle. Sheng et al.'s **Virtual Token Counter** (VTC) instead keeps a counter $c_i$ of the service each client has received:

1. When admitting, pick the client with the smallest counter that has a waiting request, and take its earliest request.
2. Charge $w_p$ per prompt token at admission and $w_q$ per generated token after every step (the paper's experiments use $w_p = 1$, $w_q = 2$, following output-token pricing).
3. **Counter lift**: when a client with nothing queued sends a request, raise its counter to the smallest counter among clients in the queue (or to the last departed client's, if the queue is empty). Idle time cannot be banked.

The paper proves the service gap between two clients that both always have work waiting stays below $2\max(w_p L_{input}, w_q M)$, where $L_{input}$ is the longest prompt and $M$ the most tokens that fit in a running batch, however long the interval.

blocks.title: VTC with three clients, 2 slots (script-computed trace)

scenes.caption: Step 0. Client A queued 6 requests (100-token prompts), client B one (40 tokens); all outputs are 10 tokens. Counters tie at 0, A goes first (+100), then B has the smaller counter and takes slot 2 (+40).

Step 10. Both finish after 10 tokens, each adding 2 per token: A 120, B 60. Only A has requests waiting, so A takes both slots (220, then 320). VTC is work-conserving: B is not owed a slot it does not use.
Step 12. B sends a new request. B had nothing queued, so its counter is lifted from 60 to the smallest counter in the queue, A's 328. Without the lift, B could cash in its idle time and lock A out.
Step 20. A's two requests finish (A at 360). B, at 328, is picked first (+40 = 368), then A (360 < 368, +100 = 460).
Step 25. Client C arrives with one request (60 tokens) and is lifted to 470, A's counter, the smallest among clients in the queue.

Step 30. Two slots free. A's running request kept adding 2 per token (A at 480), so C at 470 goes first (+60 = 530), then A (+100 = 580). A newcomer gets its share at once, without starving the heavy user.

blocks.md: Explicit **priority** is the simplest policy of all, and vLLM ships it: start the server with `--scheduling-policy priority` and each request carries an integer `priority` (lower value means earlier handling, arrival time breaks ties). When the KV pool runs dry, the preemption victim is the running request with the largest priority value, the latest arrival among equals. A common use is priority 0 for interactive chat and a larger value for batch jobs, so batch work fills idle capacity and is the first to be preempted.

Two research directions extend these ideas. **Andes** (Liu et al.) notices that users read a stream at a limited pace: in their measurements vLLM delivered about 11.2 tokens/s per request during a load surge while users read about 4.8, yet average TTFT reached 10.4 s. A preemptive scheduler that serves each request just fast enough to stay ahead of its reader can admit waiting requests sooner; the paper reports up to 4.7x better quality of experience on the same GPUs. **Llumnix** (Sun et al.) schedules across many engine instances by **live migration**: because the KV cache is append-only, it copies a request's finished blocks to another instance while decoding continues, then pauses only to copy the last iteration's blocks, for load balancing, defragmentation and priorities.

Any policy that reorders the queue (SJF, predicted lengths, priority) can starve the requests it keeps pushing back. Production schedulers pair it with an aging rule, a promotion after too many skipped steps, or a fairness counter. And under on-demand allocation a high-priority arrival can trigger preemptions, which cost recomputation (lesson 6).

Admission decides whether a request fits; ordering decides who waits. FCFS is simple but lets long jobs block short ones. SJF by predicted rank cuts mean latency, VTC shares service fairly between clients, and explicit priorities protect interactive traffic, each with a guard against starvation.

blocks.question: You run a shared API. One customer submits thousands of long batch jobs at once, and the other customers' chat requests start timing out. You do not want to reject work when the GPU is idle. Which policy fits best?
options: FCFS with a larger KV pool
Per-client fair scheduling such as VTC, which admits from the least-served client
Strict per-customer request rate limits
Shortest-job-first by predicted output length alone
blocks.explain: VTC orders admissions by service received, so the flooding customer cannot crowd out the others, and when nobody else is waiting it still gets the whole GPU. Rate limits also isolate customers but turn work away when capacity is free. SJF helps short requests but is not fair across customers, and a bigger pool does not change the order.

blocks.question: Why does VTC lift a newly active client's counter to the smallest counter in the queue instead of leaving it at its old, low value?
options: So the client cannot spend service it did not use while idle and then lock out the clients that kept the server busy
Because counters must be reset to zero after every request
To make the newcomer wait until everyone else is served
Because prompt tokens are charged twice
blocks.explain: A client that was idle for an hour would otherwise have a far smaller counter and win every admission until it caught up, starving the others. Lifting to the queue's minimum puts it on equal footing immediately, which is the paper's "credits cannot be carried over" rule.

Every production engine has the roles from lesson 1, but they draw the boundaries differently. The figure keeps the boxes fixed and swaps in each engine's own component names, taken from their docs and source code. Details change between releases; the roles do not.

The SGLang box mentions a **radix tree** cache. A radix tree is a prefix tree (a trie) whose edges hold runs of tokens: requests whose prompts start the same way share one path from the root, so the KV for that shared prefix is stored once and found by walking the tree. It is how SGLang does prefix caching.

blocks.md: **vLLM.** The engine core's scheduler hands each request a share of a per-step token budget, with no hard split between prefill and decode, so chunked prefill, prefix caching and speculative decoding all fit one mechanism. **Speculative decoding** lets a cheap draft propose several next tokens that the model then checks in one forward pass, keeping the ones it agrees with. Each of the three only changes how many tokens a request computes in a step. Scheduling is FCFS by default, or by priority with FCFS as tie-breaker (lesson 7). `KVCacheManager` allocates from a `BlockPool` created at startup. When `allocate_slots` fails, the scheduler preempts the lowest-priority running request (the last one under FCFS), frees its blocks and puts it back in the waiting queue to be recomputed.

**SGLang.** Its source describes two levels of memory pool: `ReqToTokenPool` maps each request to its token locations, and a token-to-KV allocator manages indices into the physical KV cache. Freed KV stays in the `RadixCache` tree for reuse until evicted. Admission uses the estimated-future-tokens rule from lesson 6, and decode retraction handles overflow. Since v0.4 the scheduler runs one batch ahead (the team calls it a zero-overhead batch scheduler), hiding CPU work such as radix tree matching behind GPU compute (the timeline in lesson 1).

**TensorRT-LLM.** The KV cache is a pool of blocks; tokens per block is a power of two, all layers of a token range share a block, and GQA models get blocks sized for their KV heads only. A `CapacityScheduler` (default policy `GUARANTEED_NO_EVICT`) reserves resources, then a `MicroBatchScheduler` builds the step's batch, prioritizing requests already generating. Filled blocks enter a radix search tree for reuse across requests, evicted by priority, then least recently used, and can be offloaded to secondary memory instead of dropped.

When tuning any of the three, find the same four numbers: KV pool size (gpu_memory_utilization or free_gpu_memory_fraction), max sequences per step (max_num_seqs or max_batch_size), max tokens per step (max_num_batched_tokens or max_num_tokens) and block size. Most performance surprises are one of these limits binding when you did not expect it.

blocks.prompt: Your vLLM logs keep warning that sequences are preempted in RECOMPUTE mode because there is not enough KV cache space, and p99 latency (the 99th percentile: 99% of requests are faster) is bad. GPU compute is not saturated. What would you try first?
blocks.reveal: Give the KV cache more room or ask for less of it at once, as vLLM's docs suggest: raise `gpu_memory_utilization` if it was set below its default, or lower `max_num_seqs` or `max_num_batched_tokens` so fewer sequences grow at the same time, or add tensor or pipeline parallelism to spread the weights. Each preemption throws away KV and redoes a prefill, so removing them often improves both tail latency and throughput.

blocks.md: Strip away names and every engine is the same loop: a scheduler spending a per-step token budget, a block allocator answering whether it fits, and a policy for when it does not. The engines differ mainly in that last policy and in how they reuse cached blocks.

blocks.question: Which statement about the three engines is accurate according to their documentation?
options: All three swap preempted KV caches to CPU memory by default
SGLang keeps every running request's full max_new_tokens reserved until it finishes
vLLM V1 runs prefill and decode in separate scheduler queues with separate budgets
TensorRT-LLM's default capacity policy never pauses a request once started, while vLLM V1 recomputes preempted requests
blocks.explain: GUARANTEED_NO_EVICT is TensorRT-LLM's default and guarantees started requests are not paused; vLLM V1 recomputes by default and removed CPU swapping for preemption. SGLang counts running requests' remaining tokens at an estimated ratio rather than their full maximum, and vLLM V1 uses one unified token budget.

blocks.question: A deployment serves a chat app where most requests share a long system prompt. Which component from the figure is responsible for turning that into saved prefill work?
options: The prefix cache index (hash table, radix tree or block-reuse tree)
The frontend process
The model executor
The capacity scheduler's no-evict policy
blocks.explain: The cache index finds blocks whose keys and values were already computed for the same prefix, so the new request's prefill skips those tokens. The PagedAttention and prefix caching course covers how vLLM's block hashes and SGLang's radix tree do this.

lessons.title: Build it yourself: a small engine with a block manager

blocks.md:
Several figures in this course came from simulations you never saw. In this lesson you write one: about 110 lines of plain Python that run anywhere, no GPU needed. It has requests with a hidden output length, a block manager that plays lesson 1's KV cache manager by answering "does it fit?", and a scheduler whose `step()` spends a token budget, runs decodes first, chunks prefills and preempts by recompute. A cost model turns each step into milliseconds, so you get TTFT and ITL out.

Start with the data. A request knows its prompt length, its true output length (the simulator knows it, the scheduler must not use it) and the client's `max_tokens` cap. `need()` is how many tokens must be computed before the next token can be sampled: the whole prompt at first, 1 per step while decoding, and prompt plus generated tokens after a preemption threw the cache away.

blocks.caption: Requests and a block manager with a free list. can_allocate only compares counts, the integer test from lesson 5.

blocks.code:
class Scheduler:
    def __init__(self, bm, budget, max_seqs, reserve=False):
        self.bm, self.budget, self.max_seqs = bm, budget, max_seqs
        self.reserve = reserve  # Orca-style: hold prompt+max_tokens
        self.waiting, self.running = deque(), []
        self.preemptions = 0

    def target(self, r, n):     # tokens r's blocks must hold
        return r.prompt + r.max_tokens if self.reserve else r.done + n

    def preempt(self, victim):  # recompute: drop all its blocks
        self.running.remove(victim)
        self.bm.free_all(victim)
        victim.done = 0
        self.waiting.appendleft(victim)
        self.preemptions += 1
blocks.caption: The scheduler's state. With reserve=True it behaves like Orca, holding blocks for prompt plus max_tokens from admission; otherwise blocks follow the tokens actually computed. preempt is recompute: free everything, reset progress, go to the front of the queue.

blocks.title: One step() with a preemption (block size 4, 6 blocks, budget 16)
blocks.code:
def step(self):
    batch, left, evicted = [], self.budget, False
    for r in list(self.running):          # running first
        if r not in self.running or left == 0:
            continue
        n = min(r.need(), left)
        while not self.bm.can_allocate(r, self.target(r, n)):
            self.preempt(self.running[-1])  # latest admitted
            evicted = True
            if r not in self.running:
                break
        if r in self.running:
            self.bm.allocate(r, self.target(r, n))
            batch.append((r, n)); left -= n
    while (self.waiting and left > 0 and not evicted
           and len(self.running) < self.max_seqs):
        r = self.waiting[0]                # FCFS, no skipping
        n = min(r.need(), left)
        if not self.bm.can_allocate(r, self.target(r, n)):
            break
        self.waiting.popleft(); self.running.append(r)
        self.bm.allocate(r, self.target(r, n))
        batch.append((r, n)); left -= n
    return batch

scenes.caption: Before this step: A (prompt 6), B (prompt 3) and C (prompt 5) have each generated 3 tokens and all 6 blocks are taken. A goes first: computing 1 more token means holding 9 tokens, 3 blocks, but it has 2.
No block is free, so the latest admitted request, C, is preempted: its 2 blocks go back to the pool, its progress resets to 0 and it joins the front of the waiting queue.
A is still running, so it gets a block (C's old block 3) and joins the batch.
B needs to hold 6 tokens, which its 2 blocks already cover, so no new block is needed.
The loop reaches C, which is no longer running, and skips it.
A preemption happened, so nothing is admitted this step, the rule from lesson 6. The batch is A and B, one token each.
scenes.output: C must now recompute 5 + 3 = 8 tokens, which needs 2 blocks. Only 1 is free, so C keeps waiting until A or B finishes.

blocks.md: Three decisions in `step()` carry the course. Running requests are served first, so a decode is never starved by new prompts (lesson 2). The victim is `running[-1]`, the latest admitted, and it is always at or after the request being served, so nothing already in the batch is evicted (lesson 6). And the admission loop is plain FCFS: it stops at the first waiting request that does not fit instead of skipping ahead, which would starve large prompts (lesson 7).

blocks.caption: The cost model from the GPU course (weights read once per step, or 2N FLOPs per token, whichever is slower; KV reads ignored) and the event loop. A token is sampled when a request's computed tokens catch up with prompt plus generated.

# Exercises 2 and 3: reservation vs on demand, and a shrinking pool
def workload(seed=0, n=400, rate=20.0):
    rng, t, reqs = random.Random(seed), 0.0, []
    for i in range(n):
        t += rng.expovariate(rate)               # Poisson arrivals
        cap = rng.choice([512, 1024, 2048])
        out = min(cap, 1 + int(rng.expovariate(1 / 300)))
        reqs.append(Request(i, t, rng.randint(64, 1024), out, cap))
    return reqs

def report(name, num_blocks, reserve):
    reqs = workload()
    sched = Scheduler(BlockManager(num_blocks, 16), 2048, 256, reserve)
    steps, avg_running = simulate(reqs, sched)
    ttft = sorted(r.first - r.arrival for r in reqs)
    makespan = max(r.end for r in reqs)
    print(f"{name:22s} running {avg_running:6.1f}  "
          f"p50 TTFT {ttft[len(ttft)//2]:6.2f} s  "
          f"done in {makespan:6.1f} s  preempted {sched.preemptions}")

report("reserve, 4096 blocks", 4096, True)
report("on demand, 4096 blocks", 4096, False)
for blocks in (2048, 1024):
    report(f"on demand, {blocks} blocks", blocks, False)

on demand, 4096 blocks running   39.6  p50 TTFT   0.11 s  done in   32.4 s  preempted 51
