The direction of lesson 6's bars comes back from your own code: allocating on demand runs more sequences at once (39.6 against 30.8), cuts median TTFT from 3.46 s to 0.11 s and finishes the same work sooner, at the price of 51 preemptions. Halve the pool and halve it again, and preemptions climb to 145 and 189 while median TTFT grows to 4 s and 13.6 s: frequent preemption is the symptom of a pool too small for the load.

blocks.prompt:
Evict the unscheduled request with the most blocks, which frees the most memory:

```
scheduled = [x for x, _ in batch]
cands = [x for x in self.running if x not in scheduled]
self.preempt(max(cands, key=lambda x: len(x.blocks)))
```

At 2,048 blocks, do preemptions and latency rise or fall?
blocks.reveal: In this simulator, preemptions fall from 145 to 129, because each eviction frees more blocks. Everything users feel gets worse: median TTFT rises from 3.99 s to 5.61 s, p99 end-to-end latency from 18.35 s to 23.27 s, and the run ends at 43.2 s instead of 38.3 s. The biggest request has the most computed tokens, so evicting it throws away the most work, and its recompute then occupies the token budget (lesson 6). Counting preemptions alone would pick the wrong policy.

blocks.md:
Real engines have the same shape. [nano-vllm](https://github.com/GeeeekExplorer/nano-vllm), a vLLM re-implementation in about 1,200 lines of Python, has a `Scheduler` with `waiting` and `running` queues and a `BlockManager` with `can_allocate`, `allocate`, `deallocate`, `can_append` and `may_append`, plus block hashes for prefix caching. It makes different choices from ours: a step is either all prefill or all decode, prefill steps go first whenever something is waiting, and only the first prompt in a step may be chunked. Its preemption also evicts `running.pop()`, the latest.

In vLLM the roles map to `Scheduler.schedule`, `KVCacheManager.allocate_slots` and `free`, and a `BlockPool` with `get_new_blocks`, `free_blocks` and `get_num_free_blocks`, wrapped in the many features (prefix caching, hybrid groups, speculative tokens) the other courses cover.

Extend the simulator to answer your own questions: add a per-step CPU overhead and watch ITL at batch 1 (lesson 1), add a priority field and the vLLM victim rule (lesson 7), or count recomputed tokens to see how much of the budget preemption really costs.

An LLM engine is a loop: pick requests under a token budget, ask a block allocator whether each fits, evict when it does not, run one forward pass, sample, repeat. Writing it yourself makes every knob in this course something you can test.

blocks.question: In the engine, a step preempted a request. Why does the admission loop not run in that same step, even if blocks are free afterwards?
options: Python cannot modify the waiting deque inside a for loop
Free blocks after a preemption belong to the victim and cannot be reused
Memory just ran out, so admitting a new request would likely force another preemption soon; the freed blocks go to running requests first
Admission only runs on even steps
blocks.explain: The pool just proved too small for the running set. Admitting new work immediately would invite the next preemption and repeated recomputation. The vLLM paper and this engine admit nothing while preempted work is pending in that step.

blocks.question: Spot the bug: a variant of step() loops over the waiting queue first, admitting prefills until the budget is used, and only then schedules decodes for running requests. What goes wrong under load?
options: Running requests can get no token in steps where prompts consume the budget, so their ITL spikes while new requests prefill
Nothing, the order inside a step does not matter
Prompts can no longer be chunked
The block manager loses track of free blocks
blocks.explain: The budget is spent in order. Serving waiting prompts first lets a burst of arrivals take the whole budget, and decodes stall for one or more steps. Scheduling running requests first, as vLLM does with chunked prefill, keeps every decode at one token per step.
